author: kevinpet
cardQuote: With fiverr, you have money you want to spend, and you go looking through things people imagine someone might want to pay them to do.
quote: Let me briefly explain the difference: With mturk, you have work you want to get done, and people go look through the HITs for things that fit their abilities. With fiverr, you have money you want to spend, and you go looking through things people imagine someone might want to pay them to do. I've used mechanical turk for annotating a training set for automated classification. I cannot imagine what I would use this service for. Claiming this is what mturk should have been assumes that mturk sucks because all the tasks people want to get done are boring.
storyTitle: Fiverr: What Amazon's Mechanical Turk Should Have Been Like
outcome: IPO'd on the NYSE in 2019 and built a freelance marketplace with $431M in 2025 revenue.
outcomeDetail: Fiverr listed on the NYSE in June 2019 and grew into a global marketplace for freelance services, reporting $431 million in revenue for 2025. The $5 gigs that seemed like a novelty became a broad marketplace for design, marketing, programming, and video work.
note: kevinpet could not imagine a use for Fiverr's reverse marketplace, but buyers eventually used it for everything from logos to full projects. The company turned the $5 gimmick into a public business.

author: ar7hur
cardQuote: I can't help wondering how investors can base their analysis on an experiment restricted to Palo Alto, Mountain View and San Jose.
quote: Congrats to the team! I respect what you've done so far, but I can't help wondering how investors can base their analysis on an experiment restricted to Palo Alto, Mountain View and San Jose. From what I see, the bulk of orders (in $) are from fellow startups ordering lunch and dinners. Where else is the world (except SF and maybe NYC) do so many companies, in such a small geography, order so much food from restaurants? I'm not saying it's not a good business. I'm wondering if there is really room for growth (a growth big enough to justify the huge series A valuation) outside of very specific geographies.
storyTitle: DoorDash (YC S13) Raises $17.3 Million From Sequoia To Expand On-Demand Delivery
outcome: Became the largest U.S. food delivery platform and went public in 2020.
outcomeDetail: DoorDash expanded from a Palo Alto lunch experiment into the leading U.S. delivery platform with 56% market share, and it went public in December 2020. It now operates in multiple countries and reported $13.7 billion in 2025 revenue.
note: ar7hur doubted the model could scale beyond a few tech-heavy Bay Area cities; DoorDash proved the geography objection wrong and turned delivery into a national utility.

author: OGinparadise
cardQuote: But Instacart doesn't have a choice, sending someone to deliver you a $5 ice cream isn't sustainable

Solution is to give his money back (maybe pro-rated) or honor the original deal. But Instacart doesn't have a choice, sending someone to deliver you a $5 ice cream isn't sustainable
outcome: IPO'd in 2023 and agreed to a $17B acquisition by DoorDash in 2026.
outcomeDetail: Instacart went public on Nasdaq in September 2023 and reported $3.38 billion in revenue for 2024. In October 2026, DoorDash agreed to buy Instacart for $17 billion.
note: OGinparadise was right that delivering a $5 ice cream is expensive, but Instacart built membership fees, advertising, and scale into a profitable business.

author: jasonkester
cardQuote: The race to the bottom finished years ago, and the result is that there are simply no good developers or designers left there.
quote: As a rule, you can toss every response you get in the first hour. As you've noticed, there are tons on people on those sites who send out the same canned proposal to every single listing. That level of attention is a good indicator of how the rest of your project will go if you're foolish enough to take one of them on. Wait a few days. If you've written a good project description (and if you're a bit lucky), you'll start to see a few qualified proposals trickle in. This is the main problem with freelancing sites. The race to the bottom finished years ago, and the result is that there are simply no good developers or designers left there. It's actually an opportunity waiting for talented newcomers, since a single person showing up and acting professionally would get the job described by this poster (and everybody else who goes there seriously looking to build something). I took the time to write up my experiences with these freelance sites a few years back: http://www.expatsoftware.com/articles/2007/09/how-to-fail-at...
storyTitle: Ask HN: Are freelancer sites (e.g. Odesk, Elance) useless?
outcome: oDesk merged with Elance, rebranded as Upwork, and went public in 2018.
outcomeDetail: oDesk merged with Elance in 2013, rebranded as Upwork in 2015, and listed on Nasdaq in 2018. Upwork reported $787.8 million in revenue for 2025.
note: jasonkester said the race to the bottom had left no good developers on freelancing sites; Upwork still built a public company with hundreds of millions in annual revenue.

outcomeDetail: Harry's grew into a $750 million consumer brand, raised $155 million at a $1.7 billion valuation in 2021, and filed to go public in 2024. Edgewell's $1.37 billion acquisition attempt was blocked by the FTC in 2020.
note: bsder said Harry's could only be a buyout target, not a real competitor to Gillette; the brand built its own factory, scaled past $700 million in revenue, and stayed independent after the FTC blocked Edgewell.

author: stickfigure
cardQuote: Many of my friends have tried Blue Apron, and not many still use them... At some point the customers are going to realize they can get all of these ingredients from the supermarket.
quote: Many of my friends have tried Blue Apron, and not many still use them. As a strictly amateur chef myself, find the business model pretty strange. At some point the customers are going to realize they can get all of these ingredients from the supermarket. And not long after that, they're going to realize that they already have most of these ingredients sitting in their fridge . My wife and I cook. We look up a random recipe that sounds tasty, make a list of ingredients we don't already have, pick those up at the store, and follow the instructions. It's not much harder than paint-by-numbers, which is what I expect almost every Blue Apron customer to realize at some point. I don't mean to say Blue Apron is a bad thing - it's training wheels for cooking, which is great! But when the training wheels come off, so does the subscription. At what point do they hit the saturation point and the customer base tops out?
outcome: IPO'd in 2017, lost most of its value, and was sold to Wonder for $103M in 2023.
outcomeDetail: Blue Apron went public at $10 per share in June 2017 and lost more than 80% of its market value within a year. Wonder Group acquired the company for $103 million in 2023.
note: stickfigure predicted churn once customers learned to buy the same ingredients themselves; Blue Apron's subscriber growth stalled and the business never escaped those unit economics.

author: dbot
cardQuote: I can't imagine buying a mattress online... I don't think the solution is a mystery-box-by-mail foam slab.
quote: We buy almost everything for the house online, but I can't imagine buying a mattress online. Is it annoying to buy in-store? Yes. But a mattress is an expensive, once-every-8-year purchase that you will use almost every day and is critical to your health. I don't think the solution is a mystery-box-by-mail foam slab. Many internet companies find success just by helping young-ish customers avoid the awkward interactions associated with traditional commerce. That's fine, but you are still paying for that "experience." Rarely do you get a better product.
outcome: IPO'd in 2020, was taken private in 2022, and was sold to Carpenter Co. in 2024.
outcomeDetail: Casper went public on the NYSE in February 2020 and was taken private by Durational Capital Management in 2022 at a fraction of its IPO price. Carpenter Co. acquired Casper in October 2024.
note: dbot doubted anyone would buy a mattress online; Casper proved the demand existed but never made the economics work, so the critic was right about the risk even as the category took off.

It can't just be a prettier website, can it?

outcomeDetail: Warby Parker went public through a direct listing in September 2021, valued at nearly $6 billion at its debut. It reported $871.9 million in revenue for 2025 and operates hundreds of stores.
note: bitcartel argued Warby Parker was just a prettier website atop the same Chinese supply chain; the brand, retail footprint, and direct listing proved there was more to the model.
